syllabusTopics: Saturated hydrocarbons (Alkanes): preparation from haloalkanes (reduction and Wurtz reaction), decarboxylation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkene and alkyne
Chemical properties of alkanes: substitution reactions (halogenation, nitration and sulphonation only), oxidation of ethane
Unsaturated hydrocarbons (Alkenes): preparation by dehydration of alcohol, dehydrohalogenation, catalytic hydrogenation of alkyne
Chemical properties of alkenes: addition reaction with HX (Markovnikov's addition and peroxide effect), H2O, O3, H2SO4 only
Alkynes: preparation from carbon and hydrogen, 1,2-dibromoethane, chloroform/iodoform only
Chemical properties of alkynes: addition reaction with H2, HX, H2O; acidic nature (action with sodium, ammoniacal AgNO3 and ammoniacal Cu2Cl2)
Test of unsaturation (ethene and ethyne): bromine water test and Baeyer's test
Comparative studies of physical properties of alkane, alkene and alkyne
Kolbe's electrolysis methods for the preparation of alkanes, alkenes and alkynes

rows.label: Concept
rows.text: Alkanes (**CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**) are made four ways. **Reduction** swaps halogen for hydrogen: RX + 2[H] → RH (Zn/HCl or LiAlH₄). The **Wurtz reaction** couples two haloalkane molecules with sodium in **dry ether** — **2RX + 2Na → R–R + 2NaX** — a carbon-doubling machine ideal for symmetrical even-carbon alkanes (2CH₃Br + 2Na → CH₃CH₃ + 2NaBr, the NEB 2024 answer) but useless for unsymmetrical targets, where three products…

rows.label: Formula
rows.text: - Reduction: RX + 2[H] → RH + HX - Wurtz: 2RX + 2Na → R–R + 2NaX (dry ether) - Decarboxylation: RCOONa + NaOH → RH + Na₂CO₃ (CaO, Δ) - Hydrogenation: CₙH₂ₙ + H₂ → CₙH₂ₙ₊₂; CₙH₂ₙ₋₂ + 2H₂ → CₙH₂ₙ₊₂

rows.text: "Alkanes are prepared by reduction of haloalkanes, Wurtz coupling with sodium in dry ether, decarboxylation of sodium carboxylates with soda-lime, and catalytic hydrogenation of alkenes and alkynes."

rows.label: Solved
rows.text: ***The Wurtz ledger*** — two methyls make ethane (2 carbons), two ethyls make butane (4): the reaction is a carbon-doubling machine, which is exactly why odd-carbon alkanes resist it.

rows.label: Derivation
rows.text: ## 1. Topic Introduction — Building the Simplest Skeletons Alkanes are the **saturated** hydrocarbons: every C–C bond is a single σ bond, every carbon is sp³, and the formula family is **CₙH₂ₙ₊₂**. Since they are chemically quiet, the interesting chemistry is **how to make them**: from haloalkanes by reduction, by the **Wurtz reaction**, by **decarboxylation** of sodium salts, and by **catalytic hydrogenation** of…  ·  ## 2. Fundamental Concepts ### 2.1 From haloalkanes — reduction - **RX + 2[H] → RH + HX** — the halogen is stripped and replaced by hydrogen. - Reagents: **Zn + HCl** (nascent hydrogen), **LiAlH₄** (dry ether), or **H₂/Ni**. - Example: **CH₃Cl + 2[H] → CH₄ + HCl**. ### 2.2 Wurtz reaction - **2RX + 2Na → R–R + 2NaX** — dry ether medium; two alkyl radicals couple.…

rows.label: Shortcut
rows.text: Wurtz = 2RX + 2Na, dry ether, even/symmetrical. Decarboxylation = soda-lime, C(n) acid → C(n−1) alkane. Reduction = Zn/HCl or LiAlH4. Hydrogenation = H2/Ni; alkyne takes 2H2.

rows.label: Quick concepts
rows.text: Route selection is the exam skill: Wurtz for symmetrical even-carbon alkanes, decarboxylation for methane (one carbon less than the acid), hydrogenation for any specific alkane.

rows.label: Key points
rows.text: Alkanes CnH2n+2, saturated sp3. Preparation: (1) reduction of haloalkane RX + 2[H] -> RH + HX (Zn/HCl, LiAlH4, H2/Ni). (2) Wurtz: 2RX + 2Na -> R-R + 2NaX, dry ether; symmetrical even-carbon alkanes; 2CH3Br + 2Na -> CH3CH3 + 2NaBr; mixed RX/R'X gives three products (limitation).…

rows.label: Universal facts
rows.text: Hydrogenation on nickel happens on the metal surface: both H atoms add to the same face (syn addition), which is why alkene hydrogenation is stereospecific.

rows.label: More practice
rows.text: **NEB-style (2m): Give one limitation of the Wurtz reaction.** — When **two different haloalkanes** are used together (RX and R′X), the coupling is unselective: three products — **R–R, R–R′ and R′–R′** — form in an unpredictable mixture, so unsymmetrical alkanes cannot be made cleanly.…

Detailed Explanation ### 4.1 Choosing the right route - Need a **specific unsymmetrical alkane**? Hydrogenation of the matching alkene/alkyne is cleanest. Need a **symmetrical even-carbon alkane**?
